title: Jobava London System
subtitle: The London's bishop, an aggressive knight, and opposite-side castling
summary: The Jobava London keeps the ordinary London's bishop-to-f4 idea but replaces the quiet 2.Nf3 with an early 2.Nc3 — a small change that turns a positional setup into a sharper, opposite-side-castling weapon built around a fast kingside pawn storm. The trade-off is real: Nc3 blocks White's own c-pawn and opens the door to structural damage if Black finds the right central trade.

metadata.historicalContext: Named for the Georgian grandmaster Baadur Jobava, who popularized this aggressive move order in modern practice; it is also associated with the French grandmaster Éric Prié. Grischuk and other elite players have since taken it up as a practical surprise weapon.

rootAnnotations.title: What this lesson teaches
rootAnnotations.body: The London System develops the bishop to f4 before the pawn chain closes it in — that idea is shared ground, covered fully in The London System, and this lesson does not re-teach it. What changes here is the move before it: instead of 2.Nf3, White plays 2.Nc3 first. That single substitution has real consequences — White reaches for e4-e5 and a kingside pawn storm sooner, often behind queenside castling, but permanently gives up the option of a quiet c4 or c3 structure, since the knight already sits on c3. This lesson is about the chess that only exists because of that one move-order choice.

rootAnnotations.title: Same bishop, different character
rootAnnotations.body: In The London System, White commits to a slow, almost universal setup and treats the position's small edges patiently. Here, White commits early to a plan and a side of the board — usually queenside castling and a kingside attack — and accepts sharper, more concrete play in exchange. Neither approach is objectively better; they ask for different things from the player behind the pieces.

annotations.body: This knight could have gone to f3, the quiet London's usual first developing move. What does going to c3 first actually change?

annotations.title: The one move that changes everything
annotations.body: Nc3 develops a piece, same as Nf3 would — but it also blocks White's own c-pawn, ruling out the calm c3/c4 structures that anchor the ordinary London and Colle systems. In exchange, the e-pawn is now free to advance to e4 without needing e3 as a stepping stone first, which is the entire engine behind this system's aggression. Every plan in this lesson traces back to that trade.
The shared idea with the ordinary London: the bishop escapes the pawn chain onto an active diagonal before anything walls it in. From here the two systems' move orders diverge for good.

A flexible, solid reply that supports a later ...d5-...Bf5 setup without committing the kingside yet. Black can also strike at the knight on c3 directly, at the cost of the dark-squared bishop — the variation here shows that structural bargain.

annotations.title: Opening the bishop's diagonal first
annotations.body: Instead of the flexible ...c6, Black prepares to pin the very knight that makes this system what it is.

annotations.title: Pinning the piece the whole system depends on
annotations.body: With White's king still on e1, this is a real, absolute pin — Nc3 cannot legally move at all right now. If White develops without addressing it, Black can simply take the knight and inflict doubled pawns on the queenside.

annotations.title: Doubled pawns after the trade
annotations.body: Black gives up the bishop pair to damage White's structure — the exact trade-off named in this opening's motifs, reached here by a bishop rather than a knight, but the same bargain either way: a permanent structural weakness for White in exchange for the two bishops and a half-open b-file for Black.
A brief return to modesty — this move supports d4 and opens the f1-bishop's diagonal before the sharper plans begin. Development finishes first; the storm comes later.

White's last remaining piece before the king reaches safety. Note that both sides now have a light-squared bishop developed outside its own pawn chain — a mirror image, and a direct confrontation is one move away.

In the ordinary London, this diagonal usually stays reserved for later, and a bishop offered a trade is often kept rather than exchanged. Here White offers the trade immediately. Why might accepting the exchange suit White's plan in this version?

annotations.title: Trading toward the attack, not away from it
annotations.body: White invites Black to trade off the dark-squared... no, the light-squared bishops. Losing a bishop pair sounds like a concession, but the coming recapture puts White's queen on an active central square with a direct path to the kingside, and one fewer minor piece for Black means one fewer defender once the pawn storm begins. This is the Jobava's temperament in miniature: activity and attacking chances traded for small structural or material niceties that matter more in quieter systems.
The queen recaptures toward the center and the kingside in one move — already better placed for the coming attack than it would be on its home square.

annotations.title: The point of the whole setup
annotations.body: Queenside castling is the move the ordinary London almost never makes, and it is the real reason this system exists: with the king safely away from the kingside, White is free to throw the g- and h-pawns forward without endangering its own king. This only works because development finished quickly enough — the price of the early Nc3 is paid back here, in tempo.

annotations.title: The pawn storm begins
annotations.body: This is the position the whole line was built for: opposite-wing castling, with White's king tucked away and every kingside pawn free to advance. Black's most natural plan — castling short — walks directly toward the coming storm, as the next move shows. The calmer alternative, shown in the variation, is to delay castling and strike back in the center instead.
The natural developing choice — but with White's king already safe on the other wing, this walks the king toward the pawns that are already advancing.

annotations.title: The calmer answer to a wing storm
annotations.body: Instead of castling into the advancing pawns, Black strikes back in the center while White's attack is still only forming. This is the standard antidote to any opposite-side pawn storm: counterplay against the enemy king or center is usually faster than trying to outrun the storm with king safety alone.

annotations.title: The storm arrives
annotations.body: The pawn kicks the f6-knight and the attack rolls forward exactly as planned: next comes h4-h5 and pieces joining behind the pawns, while Black must find a safe post for the knight and real counterplay before the position opens near the king. White's plan is concrete and fast; Black's task is to generate matching speed on the other wing or in the center, not to sit and defend.

annotations.title: What you should have noticed
annotations.body: Three lessons to carry forward: the Jobava London is defined by one move-order choice, 2.Nc3 before Nf3, which trades the ordinary London's flexible c-pawn for a faster path to e4 and opposite-side castling; a shared bishop idea does not mean a shared game plan — this lesson's attacking, concrete character is genuinely different from the patient setup in The London System; and against any early, committed pawn storm, racing to castle into it is rarely the right response — meeting it with central counterplay usually is.
